Can the "spirit of antichrist" still be present today?
Yes. Any teaching that denies that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh carries that spirit. What the fulfilled reading denies is a single figure called "the Antichrist" alive today.

John says the spirit of antichrist "is already in the world" (1 John 4:3). The fulfilled reading places John's "last hour" before AD 70. But it does not say that denial of Christ ended then. Every age has teachers who deny the Father and the Son or the true humanity and deity of Jesus. John's tests still apply. Does this spirit confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (4:2)? Does it hold to the Son (2:23)? Christians are to test the spirits (4:1) and remain in the teaching of Christ (2 John 9). This is a practical, daily vigilance about truth. It is not a hunt for a world leader.
1 John 4:2: "every spirit who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God" (WEB).
The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) confessed Christ as truly God and truly man. This is a church response to teachings that denied his full humanity or deity.

All Christian traditions agree that the spirit of antichrist is at work today. Futurists add that it will be fully embodied in one final person. Amillennialists often describe that hope as a final, intensified form of what has always been present.
Must the Antichrist be a Jewish man who pretends to be Christ, as some popular teachers say?
No text says so. John's "antichrists" were people of his own day who denied that Jesus is the Christ, not one future Jewish ruler.

Some popular teachers have claimed that a coming Antichrist will be Jewish and will pretend to be Christ. Read in context, the Bible never says this. The word "antichrist" appears only in John's letters (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7). There it names many people already active in John's time who denied that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh. John says this showed it was "the last hour" for his readers. Nothing in those verses gives a race or a nation. On the fulfilled reading, linking the word to a future Jewish leader adds to Scripture. It also risks feeding old prejudice. That claim drew public protest from Jewish leaders in 1999. The safer path is to say only what the text says: anyone who denies the Son is "antichrist".
1 John 2:18-19: the antichrists "went out from us". They were former members of John's own churches, of any background.
In January 1999 a well-known American preacher said the Antichrist would "of course" be Jewish. Jewish leaders publicly objected, and he later apologised for the offence.

Some futurists read Daniel 11:37 ("the God of his fathers") as a hint that the beast will be Jewish. Most futurists today expect a Gentile ruler from a revived Roman world. Historicists named the papacy. Amillennial writers expect a final personal opponent but give no race.
Why do so many interpreters call 2 Thessalonians 2 one of the hardest passages in Paul?
Paul refers to things he had already taught in person ("you know"). Later readers lack that oral teaching, so the details seem obscure.

Paul writes as if his readers already have the key: "Do you not remember that I told you these things?" (2 Thessalonians 2:5) and "you know what restrains" (2:6). The first readers had heard Paul teach in Thessalonica (Acts 17:1-4). We did not. So the letter feels like hearing one side of a phone call. Augustine admitted openly that he did not know what Paul meant by part of it (City of God 20.19). Many later scholars said the same. On the fulfilled reading, the fix is to set the chapter beside what the first readers did know: Jesus' Olivet Discourse, the Old Testament prophets, and the events of their own time. Read that way, much of the fog lifts. A passage that was clear to its first readers was about things they could see.
Augustine, City of God 20.19 (about AD 426): he confessed he did not know what Paul meant by "what restrains".
Paul's "you know" (2 Thessalonians 2:6) assumes shared knowledge, much like a letter between friends that says "remember what we talked about".

Futurists agree the passage is hard but say its plain words (a person seated in God's temple, destroyed at Christ's coming) fit the end of the age best. Amillennial writers often read it as a final rebel before the last day. Historicists saw it fulfilled in a long line of popes.
Does 2 Thessalonians 2 describe the rapture, the tribulation and Christ's glorious appearing all in one chapter?

Pretribulational teachers say yes. The fulfilled reading says no: Paul is correcting a false report that "the day of the Lord" had already come. He names events that had to happen before Jerusalem's judgment.

Some pretribulational writers say this chapter gives the rapture (verse 1), the tribulation (verses 3-12) and the glorious appearing (verse 8) together. But Paul's stated purpose is narrower. He tells the readers not to be shaken by a spirit, a word or a letter claiming that "the day of the Lord has come" (2:2). Then he lists what must happen first: the apostasy and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2:3). Read covenantally, verse 1 speaks of Christ's coming and the gathering of his people. Verses 3-12 describe a rebel already alive and restrained in Paul's day (2:6-7). Verse 8 describes his judgment. Nothing in the chapter speaks of believers rising to meet Christ in the air. Paul used those words in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, but he does not repeat them here.
1 Thessalonians 4:17 uses "caught up" (harpazo). 2 Thessalonians 2:1 uses "gathering together" (episunagoge). These are different words.
2 Thessalonians 2:2: the problem was a forged or misunderstood letter saying the day had arrived.

Pretribulationists see verse 1 as the rapture and verse 3 as proof that the tribulation cannot begin until the church is gone. Posttribulationists read the chapter as one event: the church gathered at Christ's visible return after the Antichrist. Amillennialists see the final return at the end of history.
What does the Greek word parousia ("coming") actually mean?
Parousia means "presence" or "arrival". It can describe an ordinary visit or a ruler's arrival. It does not by itself mean a bodily return from the sky.

Paul uses parousia for ordinary arrivals and presence: the coming of Stephanas (1 Corinthians 16:17), the coming of Titus (2 Corinthians 7:6), and his own "bodily presence" (2 Corinthians 10:10; Philippians 2:12). In Greek writings outside the Bible it often named the official visit of a king or governor to a city. So the word tells us that someone arrives and is present. It does not tell us how. On the fulfilled reading, the parousia of 2 Thessalonians 2:1 is the Lord's arrival in judgment. Scripture often pictures God "coming" in history without a body being seen. That happened when he judged Egypt and other nations. The word fits a coming in power against the city that rejected him, within that generation.
Philippians 2:12: "not as in my presence (parousia) only, but much more in my absence".
Greek papyri and inscriptions use parousia for an emperor's official visit. Cities sometimes minted coins or started new dating eras to honour such a visit.

Most interpreters accept the meaning "arrival, presence". But they note that in the New Testament the parousia "of the Lord" is a technical term for Christ's personal, visible return (1 Thessalonians 4:15-16; 1 Corinthians 15:23). Context, they say, settles it. Full preterists apply every parousia text to AD 70.
Was the Lord's coming really "near" for the people who first read the New Testament letters?
Yes. James grounds patience on the fact that "the coming of the Lord is near". The fulfilled reading takes that nearness at face value for the first readers.

James tells his readers to be patient "until the coming (parousia) of the Lord". He gives the reason: "the coming of the Lord is near" and "the Judge is standing at the door" (James 5:7-9). The comfort only works if the event was near for them. Peter says "the end of all things is near" (1 Peter 4:7). Hebrews says "in a very little while, he who is coming will come" (Hebrews 10:37). John calls his time "the last hour" (1 John 2:18). Read covenantally, these texts point to Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem and the end of the old covenant age in AD 70. So when 2 Thessalonians 2 speaks of the Lord's coming, it fits inside a time frame the whole church already accepted as close at hand.
James 5:9: "the Judge is standing at the door". This is a picture of someone about to enter.
Jesus used "near" for a coming Passover (John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55). In each case the feast came within weeks.

Futurists say "near" means the coming could happen at any time (imminence), or that it is near in God's view (2 Peter 3:8). Amillennial and historic premillennial writers often say the last days began at Pentecost, so the end has been "near" through the whole church age.
Does the Bible ever describe God "coming" when no one saw him in bodily form?
Often. The prophets describe God coming on clouds, riding to Egypt and bending the heavens. In each case he acted through armies and events in history.

The prophets regularly describe God's acts of judgment or rescue as his "coming". David says God bent the heavens and came down, with darkness under his feet, when he rescued David from Saul (2 Samuel 22:10; Psalms 18:9). Isaiah says the LORD rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt (Isaiah 19:1). That was fulfilled through Assyrian conquest, not a visible appearance. Psalms 97:2-5 pictures clouds and fire before him as mountains melt. On the fulfilled reading, the apostles were Jews who knew this way of speaking. Jesus took it up when he spoke of the Son of Man coming on the clouds (Matthew 24:30; Daniel 7:13). So a "coming of the Lord" against Jerusalem through Roman armies matches a long biblical pattern.
Isaiah 19:1 and 19:4: God "comes" to Egypt and gives it to "a cruel master". This was fulfilled through foreign conquerors.
Micah 1:3-6: the LORD comes down and treads the high places. This judgment fell on Samaria when Assyria took it in 722 BC.

Most interpreters accept that God "came" in past judgments. Futurists and amillennialists add that the New Testament also promises a final, personal, bodily return (Acts 1:11). They see AD 70 at most as a preview of that return, not a replacement for it.
How can God's "presence" mean blessing for some and judgment for others?
God's nearness blesses those in covenant with him and judges those who rebel. Ezekiel saw the glory leave a defiled temple. Jesus left the temple too, declaring it "desolate".

In Scripture, God's presence in the sanctuary was Israel's great privilege. But when the temple was filled with idols, Ezekiel saw God's glory leave it in stages, from the inner room to the threshold to the mountain east of the city (Ezekiel 8-11). Babylon's armies followed in 586 BC. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus repeats this pattern. He cleansed the temple (Matthew 21:12-13). He pronounced woes on its leaders and said "your house is left to you desolate" (Matthew 23:38). Then he walked out and foretold its fall (Matthew 24:1-2). His later "presence" (parousia) in AD 70 was a visit of judgment. Meanwhile his saving presence now lives in a new temple built of living stones, his people (1 Peter 2:4-10).
Ezekiel 10:18-19; 11:23: the glory moves from the temple to the Mount of Olives.
Matthew 24:1-3: Jesus leaves the temple, crosses to the Mount of Olives and predicts its destruction. This is the same path the glory took in Ezekiel.

Many interpreters of every school accept the Ezekiel-Jesus parallel. Futurists add that God's glory will return to a future temple in Jerusalem (Ezekiel 43:1-5). Amillennialists see that return fulfilled in Christ and the church, while still expecting a final bodily coming.
What clues in 2 Thessalonians 2 tie the man of lawlessness to Paul's own day?

Paul writes in the present tense: "you know what restrains him now", "the mystery of lawlessness is already at work", "he who now restrains". The fulfilled reading concludes that the figure was alive then.

Three phrases carry the case. First, "the mystery of lawlessness is already at work" (2 Thessalonians 2:7). Second, "you know what restrains him now" (2:6). Paul does not say what will restrain him in a later age. Third, "he who now restrains will do so until he is taken out of the way" (2:7). On the fulfilled reading, a restrainer is only needed while the one being held back is present. If the man of lawlessness were still thousands of years away, Paul's readers could not "know" what was holding him back. So the passage most naturally describes a person and a restraint active in the AD 50s, resolved before or in AD 70. B. B. Warfield, a Reformed scholar, linked the passage to Jesus' warning about the abomination in the holy place (Matthew 24:15).
"Already at work" (2:7) is the same idea as John's "even now many antichrists have come" (1 John 2:18).
Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians from Corinth about AD 50-51 (Acts 18:1-11). Jerusalem fell about twenty years later, in AD 70.

Futurists reply that the "mystery" of lawlessness was already working as a spirit, while its final person is still future. The restrainer (often taken as the Holy Spirit or the church) has worked through the whole age. Amillennialists say the same principle shows itself in every age before one last climax.
Is "our gathering together to him" in 2 Thessalonians 2:1 the rapture?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Paul uses episunagoge, a word for assembling believers on earth (Hebrews 10:25). He does not use the "caught up" language of 1 Thessalonians 4.

Episunagoge appears only twice in the New Testament. In Hebrews 10:25 it means the church's regular meeting together on earth. The related verb describes Jesus gathering Jerusalem's children like a hen gathers chicks (Matthew 23:37) and angels gathering the elect (Matthew 24:31). If Paul meant to clear up confusion about his earlier "caught up" teaching, why change the word? Read covenantally, the "gathering" is the long-promised ingathering of God's scattered people (Isaiah 11:12; 27:13; 56:8), now including Gentiles. With the old temple about to fall, believers would become one clear assembly gathered around Christ. That gathering began after the ascension and continues through the gospel. It moves outward across the earth, not upward into the sky.
Hebrews 10:25: "not forsaking our own assembling together (episunagoge)". This is a weekly meeting, not a flight to heaven.
Isaiah 27:13: a great trumpet gathers the scattered to worship on the holy mountain. Compare Matthew 24:31.

Pretribulationists and many others say verse 1 points back to 1 Thessalonians 4:17. They argue that "gathering to him" naturally means meeting Christ at his coming, whatever word is used. Posttribulationists agree it is the rapture but place it at Christ's visible return.
What is the biblical background of God "gathering" his scattered people into one?
The prophets promised that God would gather Israel's scattered people and add others to them. The New Testament says Christ died to gather God's children into one body of Jews and Gentiles.

Isaiah says the LORD who gathers Israel's outcasts will gather "yet others" to them (Isaiah 56:8). Caiaphas unknowingly prophesied that Jesus would die not for the nation only. He would also gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:51-52). Jesus spoke of "other sheep" who would become "one flock" (John 10:16). Paul explains this in Ephesians 2:11-22. Gentiles who were far off are brought near. The wall is broken. The two become "one new man" and grow into "a holy temple in the Lord". Peter gives the church Israel's titles: chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation (1 Peter 2:9-10). On the fulfilled reading, this is the "gathering together" of 2 Thessalonians 2:1. It is a new covenant assembly formed around Christ as the old order passed away.
John 11:52: Jesus would "gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad".
Acts 15:14-17: James sees Gentile conversion as the rebuilding of David's fallen tent (Amos 9:11-12).

Covenant theologians and progressive dispensationalists welcome the one-people theme. Classic dispensationalists agree that Jews and Gentiles are one in the church. But they hold that God will still gather ethnic Israel to its land in a future fulfilment of these prophecies (Ezekiel 37:21).
Why did Christians still go to the temple and synagogues before AD 70, and why does that matter?
The years AD 30-70 were a time of transition. Believers still worshipped at the temple. Its fall in AD 70 ended that overlap and made the church plainly God's one assembly.

Acts shows the apostles praying in the temple (Acts 3:1). Paul preached first in synagogues (Acts 13:5, 14; 17:1-2) and even joined a purification rite in the temple (Acts 21:26). James calls a Christian meeting a "synagogue" (James 2:2, Greek). Hebrews says the old covenant was "growing old" and "ready to vanish away" (Hebrews 8:13). It urges readers to go outside the camp to Jesus (Hebrews 13:13). On the fulfilled reading, these forty years were a transition between covenants. When Rome burned the temple in August AD 70, sacrifice became impossible, and the old meeting point disappeared. From then on, God's people were gathered in one clear assembly around Christ, the true temple.
Acts 21:20-26: thousands of believing Jews are "zealous for the law", and Paul offers sacrifice for a vow in the temple.
Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7: the temple burned on the 10th of the month Ab (or Lous), AD 70.

Most interpreters agree AD 30-70 was a transition. Dispensationalists add that a future temple will be rebuilt and used in the tribulation. Messianic Jewish believers also stress that Jewish identity in Christ remained valid after AD 70 and was not merely tolerated for a time.
Did the Thessalonians think the day of the Lord was "at hand" or that it had already come?
That it had already come. The verb enistemi means "to be present". Paul elsewhere says the Lord is near, so he was not correcting belief in nearness.

The KJV renders 2 Thessalonians 2:2 as "the day of Christ is at hand". But the Greek verb (enesteken, perfect of enistemi) means "has arrived, is present". The same verb appears in Romans 8:38 and 1 Corinthians 3:22 ("things present", set against "things to come"), in Galatians 1:4 ("this present evil age"), and in Hebrews 9:9 ("the time then present"). Paul and the other apostles did teach that the day was near (Romans 13:12; Philippians 4:5; James 5:8). So he could not be scolding them for believing it was near. On the fulfilled reading, a false report claimed the day had already happened. Paul answers that it had not: Jerusalem still stood, and certain events had to come first. Many scholars of every school, such as Leon Morris and Geerhardus Vos, accept "has come".
1 Corinthians 7:26: "the present (enestosan) distress". The same verb describes a trouble already happening.
Modern versions (ESV, NIV, NASB) all render 2:2 as "has come" or "has already come".

Nearly all modern scholars, futurist included, now accept "has come". Futurists explain it this way: false teachers said the tribulation (the start of the day of the Lord) had begun, which frightened readers who expected to be spared from it. Amillennialists think some claimed the resurrection had already happened (compare 2 Timothy 2:18).
If "the day of the Lord" means the end of the world or the rapture, how could anyone think it had already happened?

On the fulfilled reading, they couldn't. A burned-up universe could not be missed. Paul could not write a letter after being raptured. The confusion only makes sense if the day was a local, historical judgment.

2 Peter 3:10 says the heavens will pass away and the elements melt. If the day of 2 Thessalonians 2:2 were that event, no one would need a letter to learn of it. If it were the rapture, the Thessalonians would have noticed that they were still on earth. They would also have noticed that a letter supposedly from Paul came from someone who should have been taken up too. A report that "the day has come" makes sense if the day was a judgment in another place. News of it could arrive by message or letter. Read covenantally, the expected day was God's judgment on Jerusalem. A false rumour of the city's fall could easily reach Macedonia. N. T. Wright made a similar point: the letter assumes you could hear of the day by post.
Distance: Thessalonica to Jerusalem is about 1,300 km (800 miles) in a straight line. News took weeks by sea and road.
A modern parallel: before telegraphs, false reports of battles often travelled faster than true ones.

Futurists answer that the "day of the Lord" begins with the tribulation's judgments on earth. People living through those judgments could fear the day had begun. Others think the false teachers claimed a spiritualised coming had already happened, as Hymenaeus did with the resurrection (2 Timothy 2:18).
Is there only one "day of the Lord" in the Bible?
No. Scripture speaks of several days of the Lord. These include judgments on Babylon, Edom, Judah and Egypt, each fulfilled in history. Even futurist John Walvoord granted this.

Isaiah 13 announces that "the day of the LORD is near" for Babylon (13:1, 6, 9). Media and Persia fulfilled it when Babylon fell in 539 BC. Zephaniah's "great day of the LORD" (Zephaniah 1:7, 14) came on Judah when Babylon burned Jerusalem in 586 BC. Ezekiel 30:3 applies "the day of the LORD" to Egypt. Obadiah 15 applies it to Edom and the nations. John Walvoord wrote that the phrase describes any period in which God judges human sin directly, and that Israel had several such days. So the phrase names a type of event: God stepping into history in judgment. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus called Jerusalem's fall "days of vengeance" (Luke 21:22). That echoes Isaiah 61:2, and it was the day Paul's readers were watching for.
Babylon's fall in October 539 BC fulfilled Isaiah 13:17 ("I will stir up the Medes").
Lamentations 2:22 looks back on 586 BC as "the day of the LORD's anger". It is a day of the Lord already past.

All schools grant many past "days of the LORD". Futurists and amillennialists hold that these past days preview a final Day at Christ's return. They point to its link with resurrection and new creation in 2 Peter 3:10-13 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13-5:3.
Can "the day of the Lord" in Paul and Peter really stretch across a thousand years?

Some dispensational writers make the day run from the rapture to the end of the millennium. The fulfilled reading calls this a loss of the literal sense, since Paul and Peter use the same "thief" image of one day.

Dispensational writers must fit two texts into their plan. Paul's day of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5:2) comes before the millennium. Peter's day of the Lord, with the burning of the elements (2 Peter 3:10), comes after it. One solution says the day begins after the rapture and ends with the millennium, over a thousand years later. But both apostles use the same picture: the day comes "like a thief". That suggests one event, not two separated by a thousand years. On the fulfilled reading, using 2 Peter 3:8 ("one day is as a thousand years") to stretch time words whenever they cause trouble is unsound. That verse speaks of God's patience. It is not a code for reading "day" as a millennium.
1 Thessalonians 5:2 and 2 Peter 3:10 both say "the day of the Lord will come like a thief".
Psalms 90:4, which 2 Peter 3:8 echoes, compares a thousand years to "a watch in the night". It contrasts God's view of time with ours. It does not give a rule for converting units.

Dispensationalists answer that "day" can mean an era, as in "the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2). They say the day of the Lord is a long period of judgment and blessing. Amillennialists see one final day at Christ's return, so they need no stretch. Some preterists apply 2 Peter 3 to AD 70 as well.
What judgment did Paul mean when he said wrath had come "to the uttermost" on those who opposed the gospel in Judea?
On the fulfilled reading, Paul foresaw the coming judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. It fell on one generation of leaders who rejected Jesus. It is not a charge against Jewish people in any later age.

In 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16 Paul speaks of those in Judea who killed the Lord and the prophets, drove out the apostles and tried to stop the preaching to Gentiles. He says they "fill up their sins" and that wrath has come on them "to the end". This echoes Jesus' words about filling up the fathers' measure and judgment on "this generation" (Matthew 23:32-36). Read covenantally, Paul expected the old covenant city to be judged within that generation, as it was in AD 70. The point is historical and limited. Paul himself was Jewish, and so were Jesus, the apostles and the first thousands of believers. Writers across many schools rightly stress that no one may blame Jewish people of later centuries for those events.
Matthew 23:35-36: "all these things will come upon this generation". This is a judgment with a time limit.
Romans 9:1-5; 10:1: the same Paul says he has great sorrow for his people and prays for their salvation.

Many scholars see the wrath as already begun (for example, the riots and expulsions of AD 48-49) or as wrath shown in advance. Futurists sometimes link it to a coming time of trouble for Israel (Jeremiah 30:7). All responsible interpreters reject using this verse to blame Jewish people today.
Why would believers in Thessalonica be shaken by a report that Jerusalem's judgment had come?
Many were Jews or God-fearers with ties to Judea. They knew Jesus had warned of terrible suffering there, and they had suffered themselves. A false report would alarm them for fellow believers.

The Thessalonian church began among Jews and God-fearing Greeks in the synagogue (Acts 17:1-4). Some likely had family or friends in Judea. Jesus had said that the judgment on Jerusalem would bring great distress. He told his followers to flee when they saw the city surrounded (Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 24:21). The churches cared for each other across the empire. Paul was collecting money for the poor believers in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1-3; Romans 15:26). The Thessalonians had already suffered persecution (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14). On the fulfilled reading, a rumour that the great day had come would make them fear for their brothers and sisters. Paul calms them. The day has not come; the city still stands; certain things must happen first.
2 Corinthians 8:1-4: the Macedonian churches, Thessalonica among them, gave generously to Jerusalem's poor.
Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3: before the war, the Jerusalem church was warned to flee to Pella in Perea.

Futurists say the readers feared they had entered the end-time tribulation, which they had been taught they would escape. Others think they feared they had missed the Lord's return and the resurrection of believers who had died (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:13).
Why did the Reformers identify the man of lawlessness with the papacy, and why does the fulfilled reading set that view aside?
The Reformers saw the pope sitting in the church ("the temple of God") and claiming divine authority. The fulfilled reading says Paul's present-tense clues limit the passage to the first century.

Almost all the Reformers saw the papal office as the "man of sin". To them, a bishop seated in the church who claimed Christ's authority fitted "he sits in the temple of God" (2 Thessalonians 2:4). The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 25.6) called the pope "that Antichrist, that man of sin and son of perdition". In the centuries before, some who said this were burned. On the fulfilled reading, the Reformers rightly opposed false doctrine but missed Paul's time markers. The restrainer was active "now" (2:6-7). The mystery was "already at work". The subject was the judgment Jesus foretold on Jerusalem's temple. So a line of medieval and modern popes cannot be in view. That is also why Thomas Newton and other writers set aside Muhammad and the papacy.
Westminster Confession 25.6 (1646). Many modern Presbyterian bodies have since removed or revised this clause.
Henry Hammond (1653) proposed Simon Magus (Acts 8:9-24). This was one early attempt to find a first-century figure.

Historicists, including many Reformers and some Adventists, still see the papal system as the long-running fulfilment. They say "temple of God" in Paul means the church (1 Corinthians 3:16). Futurists and amillennialists expect a final individual. Roman Catholic interpreters see an end-time opponent of the church.
Who are the main first-century candidates for the man of lawlessness?
Three kinds have been proposed: a Roman ruler (Caligula, Nero or Titus), a priestly leader (a high priest such as Phannias), or a Zealot chief (John of Gischala).

If the figure was alive when Paul wrote, he should be found among the actors of AD 50-70. Political candidates include Caligula, who in AD 39-40 ordered his statue set up in the temple. They also include Nero, who was hailed in divine terms, and Titus, whose troops worshipped their standards in the temple court. Religious candidates include the high-priestly leadership that opposed the apostles, and Phannias, the last high priest, chosen by lot by the Zealots in AD 67-68. A third option is John of Gischala, the rebel leader who held the temple during the siege. On the fulfilled reading, the exact name matters less than the time and place. The figure was revealed, sat in Jerusalem's temple, and was destroyed when the Lord came in judgment.
Josephus, Jewish War 4.3.8: the Zealots choose Phannias son of Samuel as high priest by lot (AD 67-68).
Philo, Embassy to Gaius 188, 203-207: Caligula's order to put his statue in the temple (AD 39-40).

Futurists say none of these men fits every detail. No one was destroyed by Christ's visible appearing. So they expect a final Antichrist in a rebuilt temple. Amillennialists may grant first-century foreshadowings but still look for a final climax before Christ returns.
